processing: Orthodox black tea, rolled whole and fully oxidised, then fired and graded; lots appear as FTGFOP1, GTGFOP1 and SSTGFOP1.
harvest_season: Reported season runs April to November; second flush, in early summer, is the lot most often sold abroad.
appearance_dry: Dark, wiry leaf with a good share of golden tips.
appearance_wet: Even coppery-brown leaf with soft tips.
taste_profile: Rich and malty with natural sweetness and a honey-like edge, plus enough lively astringency to keep it from feeling heavy.

brewing.notes: Reviewers find it turns a little astringent past three minutes, so start under that. It works with or without milk.

vintage_note: Sold by year, flush and grade, with second flush of the latest season the usual choice. As with other orthodox Assams, it holds well for a year or two and is not sold as an ageing tea. Summer lots with stated tips cost more than plainer ones.
description:
Dikom is a garden in Dibrugarh district, in upper Assam, and a familiar name on specialist Assam lists. Its reputation rests on summer teas that are rich without being rough.

It is made in the orthodox way, so you get twisted leaf and visible golden tip rather than the granules of CTC. One seller reports that about 73% of the area is clonal, which would fit the consistency tasters describe, though it is a single claim.

In the cup it is malt first, then sweetness, with a honey note some drinkers pick out. The usual mistake is steeping by habit for five minutes; keep it near three and it stays smooth, then add milk only if you want to.

Check the year and flush on the label. Grade letters tell you about leaf and tip, and sellers' adjectives vary a lot, so tasting two lots from different years is more instructive than comparing descriptions.
history:
Little independent history of the garden is documented. One trade account dates it to 1875 and says it makes only orthodox tea through an April to November season; that account comes from promotional writing and has not been confirmed elsewhere.

The town of Dikom is better known locally as an oil and gas centre in the district, so the tea name and the place share company with a quite different industry.
